concept.name: Global macro trading
concept.definition: A top-down strategy class that takes long and short positions across equity indexes, government bonds, currencies, and commodities based on macroeconomic and political analysis - interest-rate paths, growth differentials, policy shifts, and geopolitics. It is practiced by global macro hedge funds in discretionary, systematic, and CTA forms.
concept.intuition: Instead of asking which stock is cheap, ask which country's whole story is mispriced - then express the view with the most efficient instrument: its currency, its bonds, its equity index, or its commodities.
concept.mechanics: Build theses from rates, growth, government policy, and geopolitics, then express them via liquid instruments - FX forwards, sovereign bond futures, equity index futures, and options - often with leverage. Sub-strategies are typically currency-based, interest-rate-based, or equity-index-based; CTA and systematic funds implement model-driven, frequently trend-following versions.
concept.failure_modes: Macro theses fail on timing: a correct long-run view can bleed carry and mark-to-market losses for years before paying - or never pay - and policy surprises such as central-bank pivots or capital controls gap markets against leveraged books.
concept.misconceptions: That global macro is glorified forecasting; practitioners emphasize asymmetric expression (options, defined-risk structures) and risk budgeting over point predictions, and the label covers both discretionary judgment and fully systematic models, which behave very differently.
concept.example: A manager bearish on U.S. growth shorts S&P 500 futures and goes long 10-year Treasury futures, while going long the currency of a commodity exporter whose terms of trade are improving.

citations.section: Understanding the Mechanics of Global Macro Strategies
